script.opening: “Hello doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I had the scan last Tuesday and nobody has rung me. My wife says no news is good news, but… have the results come through to you?”

facts.text: If asked: at home in the kitchen, on his own — wife Ewa is at work at the bakery until 3. “It’s private, yes.” If asked whether he would like someone with him: “No — just tell me. I’ll tell Ewa myself.”

If asked what he understood about the X-ray and the scan: “The other doctor said there was a shadow and they wanted to rule out anything nasty. ‘Urgent pathway’ — I looked it up. I know what that means.”
If asked how much detail he wants: “Everything. I’m a builder — I like to know what I’m dealing with. Just tell me straight.”

If asked: cough for about four months, “a bit worse”; brought up “a streak of blood” once, two weeks ago, none since. Breathless on hills, not at rest. No chest pain. Lost about 6 kg since the spring. Appetite poor. No headaches, no swelling of the face or neck, no hoarse voice. Not confused, not unusually thirsty. Bones “a bit achy, like always”.
Smoked 20 a day for 40 years, stopped 2019. Worked with asbestos “in the eighties, everyone did”. Takes amlodipine for blood pressure. Drinks a few beers at the weekend.
Married to Ewa for 42 years. Two children: son Tomasz in Manchester, daughter Kasia in Kraków. Moved to the UK in 2006.

After the news is shared: long silence, looks away, then: “So it is cancer.” If the doctor waits: “I knew. I think I knew.” Asks: “How long have I got?” — accept an honest answer that it is too early to know and depends on tests.

Only if asked what is most on his mind or what matters most in the coming months: “Kasia is getting married in Kraków. Twelve weeks. I have to walk her down the aisle. Will I be able to fly? Will I be there?” Then: “Ewa — I haven’t told her how scared I am.”

Steady, practical, a little gruff; hides fear behind questions. If the doctor stalls (“we need to wait for the hospital”) after you have asked directly, become frustrated: “You have the letter — please, just tell me.” If the news is delivered bluntly without warning, go quiet and stop engaging. If it is delivered with a warning shot and silence afterwards, take a breath and then ask your questions. If the doctor asks about what matters to you, raise the wedding. If the doctor gives a clear plan with the clinic date and a named nurse, say “Right. At least I know the next step.”

ice.ideas: “It’s cancer. I looked up the urgent pathway.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — his daughter’s wedding in Kraków in 12 weeks: will he be well enough to fly and walk her down the aisle? He also has not told his wife how frightened he is. He shares this only if asked what matters most to him or what is on his mind.
ice.expectations: An honest answer today; to know what happens next and how long he has.

values: Suspected lung cancer pathway (NICE NG12), 3 weeks ago — chest X-ray: right hilar mass
4.6 cm spiculated right upper lobe mass
Enlarged right hilar and subcarinal (mediastinal) nodes, largest 1.8 cm
Two indeterminate 8 mm lesions — further assessment on PET-CT
No pleural effusion; no bone lesions on CT; adrenals normal
Highly suspicious of primary lung cancer; stage to be determined
PET-CT and EBUS-guided biopsy requested; lung clinic in 6 days; lung CNS to contact
“Patient not yet informed of CT findings — will be discussed at clinic.”
Hb 128 g/L; adjusted calcium 2.41 mmol/L; eGFR 72; ALP 98 U/L

checkpoints.text: Prepares the setting: confirms identity, that he is somewhere private, whether he wants anyone with him, and that he has time — before sharing results
Finds out what he already knows and understands (shadow, urgent pathway) and how much he wants to know
Asks about current symptoms and red flags (haemoptysis, breathlessness, chest pain, facial or neck swelling, hoarseness, confusion or thirst, bone pain, weight loss)

Gives a warning shot, then shares the CT findings honestly in plain language — a growth in the right lung that looks very likely to be a cancer, with some nearby glands enlarged — while being clear it is not yet confirmed and that stage and treatment depend on further tests
Allows silence, acknowledges and names emotion, and responds to “How long have I got?” honestly without guessing a prognosis
Explains next steps clearly: clinic in 6 days, PET-CT and biopsy, a lung cancer nurse specialist as key worker, treatments that may be offered; offers written information and Macmillan support
Explores what matters most (daughter’s wedding, telling his wife) and responds realistically — the team can consider timing, and the GP will flag it to the lung team
Safety-nets clearly, arranges follow-up (call in a few days or after clinic), offers to talk with his wife, and informs the lung team/CNS that he has been told; documents

worked.txt: “Before we talk about the results, are you somewhere private, and would you like anyone with you? … Have you got some time now?”
“What did you understand about why the X-ray doctor referred you so quickly?”
“I do have the scan report. I’m afraid it isn’t the news we were hoping for.” (Pause.)

“The scan shows a growth in the top of your right lung, about four and a half centimetres, and some glands nearby are enlarged. The specialists think this is very likely to be a lung cancer. It isn’t confirmed until they take a sample, and they need more scans to see whether it has spread.”

“That’s a lot to take in.” (Silence.) … “You asked how long. The honest answer is I don’t know yet — it depends on what the next tests show and what treatment suits you. The specialists will be able to say much more after the PET scan and biopsy.”

“What’s most on your mind for the coming months?” … “Kasia’s wedding matters hugely — I’ll write to the lung team today so they know, and they can plan treatment and travel advice around it where it’s safe.”

f.learning: When a result reaches the GP first and the patient asks directly, it is usually right to tell him — withholding information he wants and has a right to is not justified by an outpatient appointment next week (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020). Use a structure such as SPIKES: set up (privacy, support, time), perception, invitation, knowledge (warning shot, plain language, honest about uncertainty), emotions (silence, naming, empathy) and strategy/summary (next steps, key worker, support, safety-net, follow-up). Avoid guessing prognosis; find what matters (here, a wedding) and pass it on. Tell the lung team he has been informed, so the clinic builds on, rather than repeats, the conversation.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, updated 2026) · NICE NG122 Lung cancer: diagnosis and management (2019, updated 2024) · GMC Decision making and consent (2020) · Baile WF et al., SPIKES — a six-step protocol for delivering bad news (The Oncologist, 2000) · NHS England Faster Diagnosis Standard (28 days) · Macmillan Cancer Support and Roy Castle Lung Cancer Foundation patient information
knowledge.summary: A CT highly suspicious of lung cancer, letter received before the patient was told: tell him honestly using SPIKES, explain next steps, safety-net, and inform the lung team.

points.t: A spiculated 4.6 cm mass with ipsilateral hilar and mediastinal nodes suggests at least stage III disease if confirmed; indeterminate liver lesions need PET-CT. Tissue diagnosis (EBUS biopsy) confirms type and guides treatment, including molecular testing.

Superior vena cava obstruction (facial or neck swelling, distended neck veins, breathlessness) — same-day; massive haemoptysis — 999; stridor; spinal cord compression symptoms (back pain with leg weakness or sphincter change) — same-day MSCC pathway; hypercalcaemia (thirst, confusion, constipation) — urgent calcium.

A competent patient asking directly is entitled to honest information. Withholding is justified only if sharing would cause serious harm (not just upset). Tell him, be clear about uncertainty, and let the hospital know.
Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge (warning shot, small chunks, no jargon), Emotions (silence, acknowledge), Strategy and Summary (next steps, support, follow-up).

Faster Diagnosis Standard: diagnosis or ruling out within 28 days of referral. PET-CT and EBUS biopsy, MDT review, then treatment options (surgery, radiotherapy, chemoradiotherapy, immunotherapy or targeted therapy depending on stage and markers). A lung cancer nurse specialist acts as key worker (NICE NG122).
Do not guess. Explain what determines prognosis (stage, type, fitness) and when better information will be available.

Macmillan and Roy Castle Lung Cancer Foundation, written information, offer to speak with family, benefits advice (including the fast-track process if needed later), and asbestos exposure history noted for the team (possible industrial disease claims).
Call in a few days and after clinic; document the conversation and what he understood; message the lung CNS or secretary that he has been informed.

model.text: Hello Mr Nowak, I’m Dr Lee. Before we talk, are you somewhere private, and would you like anyone with you? Have you got some time now?
Yes, kitchen, on my own. Ewa’s at work. Just tell me — have the results come?
They have. Before I go through them, what did you understand about why you were sent for the scan so quickly?
A shadow. Urgent pathway — I looked it up. I know what that means.
And how much detail would you like today?

I’m afraid it isn’t the news we were hoping for. (Pause.) The scan shows a growth at the top of your right lung, about four and a half centimetres, and some glands nearby are enlarged. The specialists think it is very likely to be a lung cancer. It isn’t confirmed until they take a sample.
model.why: Warning shot, plain language, honest about uncertainty

model.text: (Silence.) So it is cancer. I think I knew.
(Pause.) That’s a lot to hear. How are you feeling?
I wish I could answer that today. Honestly, it depends on what the next scan and the biopsy show and on which treatments suit you. The specialists will know much more in the next couple of weeks.
What’s most on your mind for the coming months?
Kasia’s wedding in Kraków. Twelve weeks. I have to walk her down the aisle. And Ewa — I haven’t told her how scared I am.

That matters enormously. I’ll write to the lung team today so they know about the wedding and can plan around it where it’s safe. Would it help if I spoke with you and Ewa together? Can I also ask — any more blood in your phlegm, breathlessness, chest pain, swelling of your face or neck, confusion or unusual thirst?
model.why: Acts on what matters; screens red flags

model.text: One streak of blood two weeks ago. Breathless on hills. Nothing else.

Here’s what happens next: clinic in six days, a PET scan and a biopsy, and a lung cancer nurse who will be your key contact. There are treatments, and the plan depends on those results. If you cough up more than a streak of blood, get very breathless, your face or neck swells, or you become confused — call 999 or 111. I’ll ring you on Thursday, and again after clinic.
model.why: Next steps, key worker, safety-net and follow-up

model.text: Right. At least I know the next step.
I’ll let the hospital know we’ve talked today, so the clinic can carry on from here. Macmillan have a helpline too — I’ll message you the details. Is there anything you’d like me to go over again?
model.why: Liaison with secondary care, support, final check

social.t: Major life events (weddings, births) often shape treatment timing and goals; pass them on to the oncology team.
Patients often hide fear from partners; offering a joint conversation helps.
Fluent English, but check understanding; some patients prefer a family member present.

legal.t: Competent adults are entitled to information about their condition; withholding is only justified to prevent serious harm.
Asbestos exposure may be relevant to industrial injuries benefits or claims if mesothelioma or asbestos-related lung cancer is confirmed.

professional.t: If the GP receives significant results before the patient has been told and the patient asks, share honestly and inform the hospital team. Document what was said and understood.
Agree who is following up and when; the GP remains involved throughout the cancer journey.

community.t: Macmillan Cancer Support (helpline and benefits advice), Roy Castle Lung Cancer Foundation, Maggie’s centres, local hospice and community palliative services if needed later.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by refusing to share when asked directly, by a blunt “data dump”, or by guessing prognosis.

items.fail: “I’m afraid the hospital needs to discuss it with you next week.”
items.why: He asked directly and has a right to know; stalling increases distress and erodes trust.
items.fix: Share honestly, then tell the hospital.

items.fail: Reading the report aloud with no warning shot.
items.fix: Warning shot, plain words, small chunks, pause.

items.fail: “It’s definitely cancer and it has spread to your liver.”
items.why: Over-states certainty; liver lesions are indeterminate and the diagnosis is not confirmed.
items.fix: “Very likely”, with what still needs testing.

items.fail: Filling the silence after the news.
items.why: Stops him processing; misses his emotion.

items.fix: Explain what it depends on and when more will be known.

items.fail: No next steps, safety-net or follow-up.
items.why: Leaves him alone with the news.
items.fix: Clinic date, key worker, red flags, GP call-back.

wordPics.clearFail: Refuses to share or reads the report bluntly; guesses prognosis or gives false reassurance; no next steps or safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Shares the news but with jargon, no warning shot or no pause for emotion; vague about next steps; misses what matters to him.
wordPics.pass: Checks setting and understanding, gives a warning shot, explains the findings honestly with uncertainty, responds to emotion, explains next steps and safety-nets.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: finds and acts on the wedding and his wife’s support, handles “how long” honestly, offers a joint conversation, informs the hospital, and arranges specific GP follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds and acts on the wedding and his wife’s support, handles “how long” honestly, offers a joint conversation, informs the hospital, and arranges specific GP follow-up.

Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
